1.0: DOCUMENT: Fundamental tensions between emergence and reductionism in complex systems theory
1.1: ASSERTS: The central tension concerns whether wholes are genuinely 'more than the sum of their parts' or whether this is an epistemological illusion masking inability to track all parts
2.1: ASSERTS: Complex systems produce novel properties (consciousness from neurons, market crashes from individual trades) that cannot be predicted even with complete knowledge of components and rules
2.2: ASSERTS: Strong emergence posits ontologically new causal powers
2.3: ASSERTS: Weak emergence accepts that higher-level patterns are in principle derivable but computationally intractable
3.1: ASSERTS: All phenomena reduce to lower-level mechanisms
3.2: ASSERTS: Nothing 'truly new' appears; apparent emergence reflects incomplete analysis
3.3: ASSERTS: Given sufficient computational power and initial conditions, higher-level behavior should be deducible from fundamental laws
4.1: ASSERTS: The most accepted reconciliation path among philosophers and complexity scientists is pragmatic pluralism
4.2: ASSERTS: Levels of description are real and useful without requiring ontological breaks
4.3: ASSERTS: A traffic jam is 'real' and has its own dynamics, even though it supervenes on individual vehicle positions
4.4: ASSERTS: The jam exhibits patterns (stop-and-go waves) best described at its own scale, yet remains consistent with physics
5.0: DOCUMENT: The causal role of organizational structure
5.2: ASSERTS: How components are arranged creates constraints and possibilities that don't exist for isolated parts
5.3: ASSERTS: The architecture itself does explanatory work—not by violating lower-level laws, but by determining which of countless micro-compatible states the system explores
6.1: ASSERTS: The productive view treats emergence and reduction as complementary tools, not metaphysical rivals
6.2: ASSERTS: Different questions demand different grain sizes
6.3: REJECTS: Insisting every explanation drill down to quarks is unproductive
6.4: REJECTS: Mystifying higher-order patterns is unproductive
